title: Pygmalion Effect in Vision: Image-to-Clay Translation for Reflective Geometry Reconstruction
claim: Guiding geometry with reflection-free proxy renderings yields cleaner reflective-surface results than a strong baseline, visible in zoomed detail.
layout: 2x4 image grid, left-to-right, red zoom-in boxes with insets
description: A two-row, four-column grid of real-scene renderings. The top row shows a dark parked SUV on a street. The bottom row shows glossy dark spheres, a bust and a metal bucket on hexagonal paving. Column one is the input reflective image, with reflections on the car windshield and the glossy sphere. Column two is the clay-like rendering: a matte grey, reflection-free version of the same scene. Columns three and four are two reconstructed renderings, the baseline and the proposed method. Red rectangles mark reflective regions in each image, and enlarged red-bordered insets sit in the lower corners. The eye goes to the matte grey clay column first, then to the red zoom boxes that compare reflection detail. There is no text or arrows in the crop.
caption: By translating reflective images (a) into clay-like renderings (b) for geometric guidance, our method produces sharper, more accurate reflective-surface geometry (c) than a strong baseline (d).
abstract: Understanding reflection remains a long-standing challenge in 3D reconstruction due to the entanglement of appearance and geometry under view-dependent reflections. In this work, we present the Pygmalion Effect in Vision, a novel framework that metaphorically "sculpts" reflective objects into clay-like forms through image-to-clay translation. We then introduce a dual-branch design in which a BRDF-based reflective branch and a clay-guided branch share the same Gaussian geometry but operate through independent rendering paths. The clay-guided branch, supervised by the synthesized clay images, provides reflection-free geometric guidance that complements the photometric supervision of the BRDF branch. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets show consistent improvements in both geometry and photometric metrics. Beyond technical gains, our framework reveals that seeing by unshining, translating radiance into neutrality, can serve as a powerful inductive bias for reflective object geometry learning.
